speakers: Niels Kaastro Larsen (host, Top Traders Unplugged)
summary: Niels Kaastro Larsen and Harry Krishnan discuss zero-day options crowding, April CTA performance and the cocoa spike, then Krishnan's 'virtual warehousing' of cheap commodities. The approach buys futures at cheap curve points and pays the roll cost by selling overpriced moderately out-of-the-money calls (hedged with far calls), then converts to trend following once prices rise. Conclusions: commercial hedgers make moderate call options rich across storable commodities, and the structure caps losses at ~25% of down moves while capturing ~2/3 of rallies.

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: I would be worried about this because as soon as this sort of idea catches catches fire or wildfire, uh there tend to be distortions in the market.
claims.claim: Selling zero-day-to-expiration straddles looks very attractive in recent backtests, but once such a trade becomes popular it tends to distort the market, so the strategy is vulnerable to crowding.
claims.conditions: Fragile once the idea is widely adopted
claims.testable: partly - 0DTE data only exists for 2-3 years

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: a strangely shaped term structure volatility where very short dated protection was quite expensive.
claims.claim: Very short-dated equity protection is expensive relative to options 2-3 days out because portfolio managers with end-of-day risk limits buy zero-day options to block out risk, creating a spike at the short end of the vol term structure.
claims.direction: short-dated vol rich versus 2-3 day vol
claims.testable: yes - compare 0DTE implied vol with 2-3 day vol

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: a lot of the data is restricted. It only goes back two or three years.
claims.claim: 0DTE backtests rest on only two or three years of data, and interpolating the surface before then is unreliable because the dynamics were different, so conclusions are weak.

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: You can generate a sharp ratio well over one or one and a half doing this.
claims.claim: Selling 0DTE straddles every day produced a Sharpe ratio well above 1 to 1.5 in the 2022-2024 sample.
claims.conditions: Sample contains no major vol spike
claims.testable: yes - Sharpe quoted from a short backtest

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: But we haven't seen a major event or major volatility spike in equity land or in equity index land since 2022.
claims.claim: The good record of short-vol 0DTE strategies reflects a period without any major volatility spike; a spike would be the real test and he sees something brewing.
claims.conditions: Strategy untested through a vol event
claims.testable: partly - depends on future vol spike

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: You could fill the holes in your portfolio by buying these things a fixed cost and blocking out extreme downside scenarios for a short time.
claims.claim: Zero-day options are useful as a fixed-cost patch for tail risk in a portfolio, which is why demand and open interest at the short end soared.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen

claims.claim: The Fed has committed to a rate-cut-hope narrative and is struggling when each inflation print comes in hot, as it did with the transitory narrative, so policy may not follow the data.

claims.claim: Powell argued there is no stagflation because growth is at least 3% and inflation below 3%.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: Trend following models still positioned kind of risk on when you look at the signals we have on at the moment.
claims.claim: In early May 2024 trend-following models were still risk-on despite April reversals, entering the summer months when decent moves sometimes occur.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen

claims.claim: Diverging central bank policies create trends in currencies, a sector that had not moved for a while, from which trend followers benefited (yen, Mexican peso).
claims.testable: yes - rate differentials and FX trend returns

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: the winner this uh this month was uh the Short-Term Traders Index. They enjoyed some of that volatility
claims.claim: Short-term CTAs gained most in April 2024 (+2.4%) from the volatility, ahead of the trend index (+1.65%) and SocGen CTA index (+1.82%).

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: uh MSCI World down 3.85% still up 4 and 1/4 for the year.
claims.claim: In April 2024 CTA indices rose while MSCI World fell 3.85% and world government bonds fell 1.77%, showing trend following diversified stock and bond losses.
claims.indicator: SocGen CTA Index, MSCI World, world govt bonds

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: cocoa seemed to be one of the markets where managed money was as large in terms of open interest um as commercial hedging activity was, both for producers and end users.
claims.claim: In cocoa managed-money open interest was as large as commercial hedging, which is unusual and suggests a major piling into the trend trade.
claims.indicator: CFTC Commitments of Traders: managed money vs commercial open interest
claims.conditions: Illiquid market with small open interest

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: because managed money typically correlates to trend in most markets.
claims.claim: Managed-money positioning in the COT report typically correlates with trend, so it can be used as a proxy for trend-following crowding.
claims.testable: yes - correlate managed-money positions with trend signals

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: And cocoa was a phenomenal market in so many ways. One is that it had long periods where it hadn't trended.
claims.claim: Cocoa had long untrended periods and is not very liquid, so some trend followers may not have included it in their basket and missed the later trend.
claims.testable: partly - depends on each manager's universe

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: I don't think the trend followers interestingly enough really had much to do with with cocoa once it became a parabolic trade.
claims.claim: Longer-term trend followers got their cocoa entry signals in January 2023 and built positions slowly, so the parabolic phase in 2024 was driven by other speculators rather than by trend followers.
claims.conditions: Depends on time scale of the trend follower

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: trend followers in general who uses dynamic position sizing will have been selling cocoa all of this year because of the increased volatility.
claims.claim: Volatility-scaled position sizing makes trend followers reduce positions as volatility rises, so they were net sellers of cocoa during its 2024 spike.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: if another hedge fund bought those contracts, you wouldn't see it, right?
claims.claim: The COT managed-money category misses other funds' buying (it is blurred), so it is an incomplete measure of who is long.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: there was also news out that Nigeria actually has is going to come out out with a better harvest.
claims.claim: Cocoa fell 35% in two weeks after exchange margin increases and news of a better Nigerian harvest, ending the parabolic run.
claims.testable: partly - margin changes and supply news are datable

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: It's hard to replicate the VIX. It's very hard to store natural gas unless you liquefy it.
claims.claim: VIX and natural gas/electricity are analogous because neither can be easily stored or replicated, giving futures term structures and option dynamics that look alike.
claims.testable: yes - compare term structures and option behaviour

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: So, you get severe contango in the term structure where the front month trades at a significant discount to the further out months.
claims.claim: Non-storable markets (VIX, natural gas, electricity) show severe contango, so long positions face heavy roll-down costs.

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: So, trend longer-term trend followers, let's say, are typically short most of the time these markets.
claims.claim: Because of contango, longer-term trend followers are short most of the time in these markets and then get hurt by sporadic mega spikes from supply shortages or risk-off events.
claims.indicator: trend signal in VIX / natural gas
claims.direction: short most of the time, losses in spikes
claims.testable: yes - backtest trend on these markets

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: And so, I put all of this stuff into into my backtesting engine. And I found that the same sorts of trades seem to be working.
claims.claim: The same option trades that work in VIX also work in the storage-constrained commodities, found by transferring structures across analogous markets in a backtest.

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: So, let's say 3-month to maturity S&P puts that are 10% out of the money tend to be quite pricey because institutions like to buy them.
claims.claim: Three-month 10%-out-of-the-money S&P puts are expensive because institutions buy them for hedging and collared products, so hedging strategies can be built around selling them.
claims.direction: sell moderately OTM puts, buy far OTM

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: I found that in the commodities markets such as oil, or corn, soybeans, and so on, out of the money call options, which are trading on the other side of the distribution, tend to be expensive.
claims.claim: In oil, corn and soybeans, out-of-the-money calls are rich, the mirror image of equity puts, probably because hedgers buy them.
claims.indicator: OTM call implied vol in oil, corn, soybeans

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: uh deglobalization seems to be coming into vogue. Where countries are worried about food security, about energy security, about being able to produce what they need internally.
claims.claim: Deglobalization and food and energy security concerns require more domestic infrastructure and add frictions to commodity trade, which could push prices higher.

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: Which, as it progresses at whatever pace, will require large amounts industrial metals such as copper.
claims.claim: The green transition requires large amounts of industrial metals such as copper (e.g. rebuilding the grid), supporting copper demand.

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: Uh we're also in an environment where weather volatility seems to be picking up.
claims.claim: Greater extremes in temperature and precipitation (e.g. Brazil deforestation) destabilise grain and other commodity prices and should raise price volatility.

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: Where countries are trying to, God forbid, remilitarize, which requires a lot more metal and energy uh inputs, or requires a lot more of those.
claims.claim: Remilitarization raises demand for metals and energy.

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: in World War I and World War II, the price of wheat trebled.
claims.claim: In both world wars wheat prices rose three to four times in sustained moves, an analogy for a geopolitically driven commodity rally.

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: I do accept that technology and sort of the improved supply chains from 50 years ago or 75 years ago are creating a bit of a downward pressure on grains, at least at the top for the time being.
claims.claim: Better technology and supply chains limit how far grains can rally compared with the wars, putting downward pressure on grain prices at the top.

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: being able to own stuff that's cheap seems to be immensely valuable.
claims.claim: Owning depressed commodities with low carry and high participation if prices rise is valuable; virtual warehousing means buying and holding cheap commodities through financial instruments with low bleed.

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: there's less incentive for me, let's say if I'm a farmer and corn's at $3 to sell corn into the market to pay off my loan
claims.claim: Physical storage costs (insurance, depreciation) fall and sellers have less incentive to sell when prices are low, so holders are implicitly paid to wait.

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: on average the cost of buying and rolling a long position goes up quite dramatically as the price goes down.
claims.claim: In commodity futures the cost of buying and rolling a long position rises sharply as price falls because of curve effects, unlike fixed warehouse rental, so a physical holder and a futures holder are treated asymmetrically.
claims.indicator: futures curve roll cost vs price level
claims.direction: long futures bleed more at low prices
claims.testable: yes - roll yield vs price level

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: for long dated options you can sometimes pay for time decay using forward curve dynamics.
claims.claim: In hedging, forward-curve roll-down can pay for option time decay (rho pays for theta) when rates are below the dividend yield.

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: In the virtual warehousing world, it's the problem is similar, but almost the other way around. You pay for roll down with theta.
claims.claim: In commodities the structure is reversed: option time decay (theta) earned from selling rich options pays for the futures roll-down.

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: are highly incentivized to sell futures to lock in gains.
claims.claim: When corn rises, producers, storage and elevator operators sell futures to lock in gains; the same holds in copper, because commercial hedgers care about staying in business more than the right tail.

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: most uptrends do not accelerate in markets where commercial hedgers are selling into rallies.
claims.claim: Commercial hedging dampens rallies so moderate uptrends rarely go ballistic.

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: somewhat out of the money call options which are providing insurance against moderate outcomes moderate increases tend to be overpriced.
claims.claim: Moderately out-of-the-money calls are overpriced because hedgers sell futures into rallies, which can be shown by backtests.

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: being a seller of these moderately out of the money options can be very profitable if you can buy other options around it.
claims.claim: Selling moderately OTM calls while buying further OTM calls and covering the extreme is attractive and funds the carry of long futures.
claims.direction: short moderate OTM calls, long far OTM calls

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: So, the virtual warehousing idea is basically a combination of buying futures, targeting cheaper points on the curve to manage roll costs
claims.claim: Virtual warehousing buys futures at the cheapest curve points and funds roll costs from rich option premium so that holding a flat market costs close to zero.

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: There are a number of reasons why out of the money options are expensive but but extremely out of the money options are not
claims.claim: Moderately OTM options are rich while extremely OTM options are not, which allows selling the former and buying the latter.
claims.indicator: OTM option skew by strike distance

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: Yes. Yes. And to be fair, the warehousing works well in conjunction with trend following.
claims.claim: Virtual warehousing complements trend following: warehouse early in the move while the price is low, then switch to trend following.

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: Until the price did go up significantly, at which point I would turn into more of a trend follower.
claims.claim: Use warehousing at low prices (avoiding a short trend position and roll costs), then convert to trend following once price rises to capture the full move.
claims.indicator: price rise from a cheap level
claims.conditions: Natural gas example, as of May 2024
claims.testable: partly - rule for switch not specified

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: trend following has the marvelous quality of having a risk control mechanism built into it.
claims.claim: Trend following has built-in risk control: the position is held while the trend lasts and exits when it breaks.

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: gas is at a buck 50 uh the the risk of it's going down a dollar are far lower than the odds of it's going up by an equivalent amount.
claims.claim: At very low prices (e.g. gas at $1.50) the payoff is asymmetric to the upside, while at $6-7 the risk becomes symmetric, so the early part of a rally has the best skew.
claims.testable: yes - conditional return distribution by price level

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: if the price of a commodity is low and it drops further, I'll lose about 25% of the down move. If the price rallies, I'll capture about 2/3 of the upside.
claims.claim: The warehousing structure loses ~25% of further declines and captures ~2/3 of rallies (only ~50% of a one-day spike), a rule-of-thumb payoff.

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: So, if the spot price flatlines, the futures will typically drift down, but I won't drift down.
claims.claim: If spot is flat the long futures drift down but the combined structure stays flat because option premium offsets roll costs.

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: commodity options markets are driven by necessity as much as they are by arbitrage type ideas.
claims.claim: Commodity option prices reflect hedging necessity, creating systematic mispricing that arbitrageurs do not fully remove.

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: for all storable commodities or for nearly all storable commodities, the um same structures work.
claims.claim: The same structures work across nearly all storable commodities, giving cross-sectional stability.

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: Airlines are not that solvent some of the time. It's not been the greatest business to run. So, they're not going to be doing complicated structures that have open-ended risk.
claims.claim: End users such as airlines are credit-constrained and hedge simply by buying call options, which creates structural demand for OTM calls.

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: markets where the price is low, but the demand for out-of-the-money insurance is high. That's a good regime for me.
claims.claim: The structure works best when commodity prices are low but demand for OTM insurance is high.
claims.indicator: price level and OTM call demand

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: And the attractiveness of some of these structures decreases as prices rise and the hedging has already occurred or is being monetized.
claims.claim: As prices rise and hedging is monetised, the relative-value structures become less attractive, which is where trend following takes over.

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: Uh please remember, though, that I'm covering all the upside. I'm not just selling out-of-the-money options.
claims.claim: The structure is bounded: sell moderate OTM options, buy deep OTM and at-the-money options so all upside is covered.

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: As a hedger, my idea is to buy volatility when it's cheap, and then turn it into a trend follower if I have to provide protection on the way down once volatility has become rich.
claims.claim: In hedging, buy volatility when cheap and switch to trend following for downside protection once vol is expensive.
claims.direction: long vol when cheap, then trend following

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: volatility tends to be more cyclical than price. Prices tend to trend a lot more.
claims.claim: Volatility is cyclical (mean-reverting) while prices trend, so insurance is overpaid when vol is high and selling into the decline gives the same protection.

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: the signal-to-noise ratio in bear markets tends to be lower than in bull markets because declining markets for equities tend to be choppy.
claims.claim: Pure momentum is harder in equity indices because declines are choppy and rallies more stable.

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: And as soon as you put an options trade on, you've already decided what regime you're hoping for and what you don't want because there's no structure that will do well in every case.
claims.claim: Every option structure encodes a regime bet, so participation should be regime-based.

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: the options liquidity is sharply decreasing once you go beyond biggest 10 commodities markets, let's say.
claims.claim: Option liquidity drops sharply beyond the ten biggest commodity markets (cocoa unplayable), restricting the universe to about 10-15 markets.

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: liquidity and the ability to store the commodity are two drivers in this whole thing.
claims.claim: The edge relies on liquid options and storable underlyings, so it does not extend to weather derivatives.

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: things like the two cream ETFs, which are blends of futures, and you've lost the virtual storage concept immediately.
claims.claim: Physically backed ETFs (gold) give real storage but blended futures ETFs lose it through roll costs, leaving a gap the strategy fills.

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: your break-even for corn has historically been $4 over 12-month horizon. It costs a dollar to buy and roll the futures at least from 2000 to the present.
claims.claim: Holding $3 corn via futures needs about $4 to break even over 12 months (30% roll cost), versus 5-10% for virtual warehousing.

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: come up with unconditional back tests across markets, see how stable the ideas are, identify the possible reasons for the mispricings in the structures that work
claims.claim: The research process is: unconditional backtests across markets, check stability, identify the reason for the mispricing, then find regimes that favour the structure.

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: templates which maps a state of the world onto a trade.
claims.claim: The strategy is systematic: each regime (trend- or vol-based) maps onto a standard trade structure.

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: there is discretion in terms of legging up the trade.
claims.claim: Execution is manual: legging into trades, choosing time of day and sourcing liquidity.

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: the sensitivity of commodity shares to say the S&P 500, or the level of diversification of certain businesses that cloud the issue of whether they're really gaining exposure to what they want.
claims.claim: Commodity equities are noisy proxies for commodity prices (hedging, diversification, passive flows, equity beta).

claims.speaker: Harry Krishnan
claims.quote: Uh oil and to a lesser extent gas because of its lack of storage.
claims.claim: Applied to copper, silver, gold, oil, some gas and grains; gas is limited because of poor storability (seven or eight markets running).
